name: Eloralintide

lead: Eloralintide is a weekly injectable amylin agonist from Eli Lilly. It selectively activates the amylin receptor, promoting fullness and slowing stomach emptying, which lowers appetite and drives weight loss for a leaner body.

A 48-week phase 2 trial in adults with obesity or overweight and a comorbidity was published in The Lancet in 2025. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports weight loss from 9.5 percent at the lowest dose to 20.1 percent at the highest, versus 0.4 percent with placebo. Lilly began phase 3 trials in December 2025.

paras: It is not available outside trials. In development it is a once-weekly injection, with weight loss building over the 48-week trial period.
Nausea and other gastrointestinal effects were the most common adverse events. It is investigational and not approved.

angle.text: Eloralintide is Lilly's weekly amylin agonist: it increases fullness and lowers appetite, leading to weight loss and a leaner body. Phase 2 trials reported roughly 9 to 20 percent weight loss at 48 weeks.

lead: Eloralintide (LY3841136) is an investigational once-weekly injectable from Eli Lilly that activates amylin receptors to reduce appetite and body weight [1][2]. Its connection to appearance runs through fat loss: appetite-suppressing drugs that lower body weight tend to slim the waist, body and face, and people who follow obesity-drug news often follow it for that reason. It is not approved for any use [1].

Amylin is a hormone released by the pancreas together with insulin after meals; it slows stomach emptying, helps end meals and dampens glucagon release [3][4]. The first amylin drug, pramlintide (Symlin), was approved by the FDA in March 2005 for insulin-treated diabetes [3]. Eloralintide belongs to a newer group of long-acting amylin agonists that also includes cagrilintide, petrelintide and others, which a 2026 narrative review describes as an emerging obesity class [5][4].

A 48-week phase 2 trial was published in The Lancet in 2025 [6]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports weight loss ranging from 9.5 percent at the lowest dose to 20.1 percent at the highest, versus 0.4 percent with placebo, and a network meta-analysis estimated an 18 percent placebo-adjusted reduction at the high dose [1][7]. Lilly began phase 3 trials in December 2025 [1][8].
infobox: About 13 to 15 days in phase 1 (per Grokipedia) [1]

paras: The programme targets adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, as a weekly injection [1][6]. Separate phase 3 trials enrol people without type 2 diabetes, people with type 2 diabetes, people with persistent obesity while on a weekly incretin drug, people with obesity and obstructive sleep apnoea, and people with obesity, diabetes and raised cardiovascular risk [9][8][10][11][12].

No study has measured facial or aesthetic outcomes. The route to a changed look is weight and fat loss; a preclinical report on rats described the weight lost as driven mainly by fat mass rather than lean mass, though the human body-composition data are still being collected [1]. Reviews of weight-loss drugs also discuss how amylin agents might offer weight loss with a different tolerability profile from incretin drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, which are well known in online appearance communities [13][5].

Eloralintide is described as selectively activating the amylin 1 receptor, with about 12-fold greater potency there than at the calcitonin receptor, which earlier analogs such as pramlintide also bind [1][2]. Amylin signalling acts on the hypothalamus and brainstem to promote fullness, slows gastric emptying and suppresses glucagon after meals [13][3]. Reviews note that these mechanisms are distinct from those of GLP-1 drugs [13][4].
A fatty diacid chain extends the peptide's half-life so that weekly injection is possible; Grokipedia reports about 13 to 15 days from phase 1 [1][2].

Grokipedia reports mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal effects, mostly nausea during dose escalation, with fatigue in some dose groups and about 10 percent overall discontinuation similar to placebo [1]. The network meta-analysis of amylin-based therapies evaluated overall and specific gastrointestinal adverse events as a secondary outcome across the class [7]. Because the drug is investigational, there is no approved label.

Amylin was characterised in the mid-1980s, and the synthetic analog pramlintide reached the market in 2005 for people with diabetes using insulin [3][4]. Its limited weight effect and need for multiple daily injections led developers to seek long-acting versions [5]. Lilly reported the discovery and first-in-human work for eloralintide in 2025, including translational studies in rats and monkeys alongside a phase 1 trial [2]. The Lancet phase 2 publication followed in 2025 and phase 3 registration began in December 2025 [6][8].

The 12-week phase 1 study and translational work have been published [2][14]. The 48-week phase 2 trial was a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled study in adults with obesity or overweight and at least one weight-related condition, testing several doses and escalation schemes of once-weekly eloralintide [6]. A network meta-analysis of six trials in 4,642 adults without diabetes ranked high-dose eloralintide second for percentage weight loss among new amylin agents, at 18.01 percent below placebo, behind amycretin and ahead of CagriSema and of semaglutide 2.4 mg and liraglutide 3.0 mg [7].

A phase 1 study combines eloralintide with tirzepatide [15], and a 2026 cardiology review summarises early data on cardiometabolic effects [16]. Registered phase 3 trials include NCT07321886 (about 1,980 participants without diabetes), NCT07282600 (about 1,035 with type 2 diabetes), NCT07392190 (persistent obesity on a weekly incretin), NCT07369011 (sleep apnoea) and NCT07900633 (cardiovascular risk) [9][8][10][11][12].

Public attention comes from the wider wave of obesity drugs after semaglutide and tirzepatide, with commentators asking whether amylin drugs could offer more weight loss with less nausea [5][13]. Reviews of next-generation therapy discuss both optimism and controversies about long-term safety, muscle preservation and cost [17]. Eloralintide has no approval, so access is limited to clinical trials.

timeline.event: Pramlintide approved in the US as the first amylin drug [3]
Phase 1 and translational data and 48-week phase 2 results published; phase 3 begins in December [1][6][2]
Additional phase 3 trials registered, including sleep apnoea and cardiovascular risk studies [10][12]
